title: Middleware & the Edge Runtime
summary: A single `middleware.ts` at the project root runs **before a request completes**, on the **Edge runtime**, letting you redirect, rewrite, gate auth, run A/B tests, handle i18n, or set headers globally — but only with Web APIs, not Node.js APIs.

subtopics.title: middleware.ts (runs before the request completes)
subtopics.explanation: You export a single `middleware` function from middleware.ts at the project root. Next runs it for matching requests BEFORE rendering/route handlers, so it can inspect the request and decide to continue, redirect, rewrite, or respond directly.

subtopics.title: The Edge runtime
subtopics.explanation: Middleware executes in a lightweight V8-based Edge runtime (Web APIs only), deployed close to the user at the CDN edge. This means very low latency and fast cold starts, but no Node.js built-ins (fs, net, native modules).
subtopics.example: // Web APIs only: fetch, Request, Response, URL, crypto.subtle…

subtopics.title: Matchers
subtopics.explanation: By default middleware runs on every request, which is wasteful. The `config.matcher` export scopes it to specific paths (with negative lookaheads to skip static assets), so it only runs where needed.

subtopics.title: NextResponse
subtopics.explanation: NextResponse is the toolkit for the response: `next()` continues, `redirect(url)` sends the user elsewhere, `rewrite(url)` serves a different path transparently, and you can set cookies/headers on the response.

subtopics.title: Redirect vs rewrite
subtopics.explanation: A redirect changes the URL the browser sees (a real 3xx the client follows). A rewrite keeps the URL but serves a different underlying path — invisible to the user — which is how you implement A/B tests, masking, and i18n routing.

subtopics.title: Auth gating
subtopics.explanation: A classic use case: read a session cookie/token and redirect unauthenticated users to /login before they ever reach a protected page. Because it runs at the edge before render, the protected page never executes for blocked users.

subtopics.title: A/B testing & i18n
subtopics.explanation: Middleware can bucket users (e.g. by cookie) and rewrite to a variant, or detect locale from headers/cookies and rewrite to a localized path — all without the browser URL changing and without per-page logic.

subtopics.title: Headers & cookies
subtopics.explanation: You can set security headers, CSP nonces, or feature flags on the outgoing response, and read/set cookies — applying cross-cutting concerns in one place instead of in every route.
subtopics.example: const res = NextResponse.next(); res.headers.set('x-frame-options', 'DENY'); return res;

subtopics.title: Limitations
subtopics.explanation: No Node.js APIs (fs, child_process, native crypto), tight execution-time budgets, and limited bundle size mean heavy work (DB queries, bcrypt, large libraries) doesn't belong here. Keep middleware fast and do real work in route handlers/server components.
subtopics.example: // Avoid: import bcrypt; do auth verification in a route handler instead.

foundations.overview: Middleware is code in middleware.ts that Next.js runs on the Edge runtime before a matched request is completed. It returns a NextResponse to continue, redirect, rewrite, or short-circuit — making it the place for cross-cutting concerns like auth gating, redirects, A/B testing, i18n, and headers.
foundations.formalDefinition: Next.js Middleware is a single Edge-runtime function exported from middleware.ts that intercepts matching requests before they reach the router/handlers, receives a NextRequest, and returns a NextResponse (next/redirect/rewrite/response) to influence the request lifecycle.
foundations.whyItMatters: It's the only place to run logic globally before rendering, at the edge, with minimal latency. It centralizes concerns that would otherwise be duplicated across pages, and it can protect routes before any page code runs.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of middleware as a programmable gatekeeper sitting at the CDN edge in front of your whole app: every matching request passes through it, and it can wave the request on, send it elsewhere, or quietly swap which page is served.
foundations.browserPerspective: For a rewrite the browser URL stays the same while different content arrives; for a redirect the browser receives a 3xx and navigates to a new URL. The browser never sees the middleware code — only its decisions (status, location, headers, cookies).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Gating /dashboard behind a session cookie, redirecting legacy URLs, bucketing users into A/B variants via rewrite, detecting locale and rewriting to /en or /fr, and injecting security headers/CSP nonces.
foundations.businessImpact: Edge-run gating and redirects cut latency and protect revenue paths (auth, paywalls); A/B testing at the edge enables fast experimentation; centralized headers reduce security risk and audit cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Cross-cutting logic lives in one tested file instead of being scattered, but engineers must respect the Edge constraints (Web APIs only) and keep it lightweight to avoid slowing every request.
foundations.performanceImpact: Middleware runs on the critical path of EVERY matched request, so it must be fast and tightly scoped via matchers. Edge execution has low latency and fast cold starts, but unnecessary matching or heavy work adds latency to all traffic.
commonUseCases: Auth gating: redirect unauthenticated users before a protected page renders
Redirects/rewrites: legacy URL handling and transparent path masking
A/B testing: bucket users by cookie and rewrite to a variant
Internationalization: detect locale and rewrite to a localized path
Security: set headers, CSP nonces, and cookies globally

commonMisconceptions.myth: Middleware can run any Node.js code, like database queries or bcrypt.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It runs on the Edge runtime with Web APIs only — no Node built-ins, tight time/size budgets — so heavy work belongs in route handlers or server components.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Middleware runs after the page is rendered.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It runs BEFORE the request completes, ahead of rendering and route handlers, which is why it can block or reroute a request entirely.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Middleware runs only where you want by default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: By default it matches every request; you must scope it with config.matcher or it needlessly runs on assets and API routes.

steps.name: Request arrives
steps.detail: A request hits the edge. Next checks config.matcher to decide whether middleware should run for this path.

steps.name: Match
steps.detail: If the path matches, middleware executes on the Edge runtime with a NextRequest (cookies, headers, geo, URL).

steps.name: Decide
steps.detail: Your code inspects the request — e.g. is there a session cookie? which A/B bucket? which locale?

steps.name: Respond
steps.detail: Return NextResponse.next() to continue, redirect() to send elsewhere, rewrite() to serve a different path, or a direct Response.

steps.name: Continue
steps.detail: On next()/rewrite the request proceeds to rendering/route handlers, now possibly with added headers or cookies.

steps.name: Page runs
steps.detail: Only after middleware allows it does the page/handler execute — so blocked users never trigger protected code.

debuggingLab.title: Middleware crashes using a Node API at the edge
debuggingLab.symptom: The app errors at the edge (e.g. 'Module not found' / runtime error) because middleware imports a Node-only library to verify a JWT.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The Edge runtime only supports Web APIs, so importing Node's `crypto` (or doing a DB query) fails or is unsupported. Middleware runs on every matched request, so heavy verification also adds latency to all traffic.
commonMistakes: Importing Node built-ins (crypto, fs) or Node-only libraries into middleware.
Doing expensive work (DB lookups, bcrypt) on the request's critical path at the edge.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Keep middleware to a cheap edge-safe check (cookie presence / lightweight JWT verify with Web crypto) and move heavy verification to a route handler/server.

theory.question: What is Next.js Middleware, when does it run, and what runtime does it use?
theory.directAnswer: Middleware is a single function exported from middleware.ts that Next.js runs on the Edge runtime BEFORE a matched request completes — ahead of rendering and route handlers. It receives a NextRequest and returns a NextResponse to continue (next), redirect, rewrite, or respond directly. Because it runs at the edge with Web APIs only, it's ideal for fast, global concerns like auth gating, redirects, A/B testing, i18n, and headers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An Edge-runtime interceptor that runs before the request is fulfilled.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To run cross-cutting logic globally and close to the user with minimal latency, before any page code executes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: config.matcher decides which paths trigger it; the function inspects the NextRequest and returns NextResponse.next/redirect/rewrite to influence the lifecycle.

theory.whyImportant: It's the only pre-render, global hook in Next, and using it correctly (and within Edge limits) is a senior-level differentiator.
theory.realWorldExample: Redirect unauthenticated users from /dashboard to /login before the dashboard renders.

nestedTopics.title: Edge runtime
nestedTopics.explanation: V8-based, Web APIs only, low latency and fast cold starts, no Node built-ins.

nestedTopics.title: Matchers
nestedTopics.explanation: config.matcher scopes execution so middleware doesn't run on every asset/request.

followUps.question: Where do you put heavy auth verification?
followUps.answer: In a route handler or server component — middleware should do only cheap, edge-safe checks (cookie presence, lightweight JWT verify).

theory.question: What's the difference between NextResponse.redirect and NextResponse.rewrite, and when do you use each?
theory.directAnswer: redirect sends the client a 3xx with a new Location, so the BROWSER URL changes and the client navigates again — used for auth gates and moving legacy URLs. rewrite keeps the browser URL the same but serves a DIFFERENT underlying path transparently — used for A/B testing, i18n localized paths, and URL masking. next() simply lets the request continue.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two NextResponse outcomes: a visible navigation (redirect) vs an invisible path swap (rewrite).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some flows must change the URL (redirect); others must keep it while serving different content (rewrite).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: redirect returns a 3xx the client follows; rewrite resolves a different internal path server-side without changing the address bar.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong breaks UX/SEO — e.g. using redirect for A/B testing exposes the variant URL and flips the address bar.
theory.realWorldExample: A/B test rewrites /home to /home-variant-b (URL stays /home); a login gate redirects to /login (URL becomes /login).

nestedTopics.title: SEO impact
nestedTopics.explanation: Rewrites keep canonical URLs stable; redirects (esp. 308/301) signal moved content to crawlers.

followUps.question: How do you persist an A/B bucket across requests?
followUps.answer: Set a cookie on the NextResponse the first time, then read it on subsequent requests to keep the user in the same variant.

scenario.question: Auth checks are duplicated in every protected page and some unauthenticated requests still briefly render protected content. How do you fix this with middleware?
scenario.directAnswer: Move the gate into middleware.ts so the session check runs at the edge BEFORE any protected page renders. Scope it with config.matcher to the protected routes, read the session cookie, and redirect to /login when missing. Because middleware runs before rendering, blocked users never trigger the protected page, and the duplicated per-page checks can be removed.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Centralizing route protection at the edge instead of per page.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Per-page checks duplicate logic and can render before redirecting (flash of protected content).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A matcher targets protected paths; middleware redirects unauthenticated requests before the page executes.

scenario.whyImportant: It removes a real security/UX bug (content flash) and consolidates logic — a common production cleanup.

nestedTopics.title: Defense in depth
nestedTopics.explanation: Still authorize data access in route handlers/server code; middleware is a gate, not the only guard.

followUps.question: Why not do the full JWT+DB verification in middleware?
followUps.answer: Edge limits (no Node APIs, time/size budgets) and per-request latency; do a cheap edge check and verify fully on the server.

coding.question: Write middleware that gates /dashboard behind a session cookie and adds a security header, scoped with a matcher.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll export a middleware function that reads the session cookie; if absent, redirect to /login preserving the intended path. Otherwise continue with NextResponse.next() and set a security header on the response. Then scope execution to /dashboard via config.matcher.
coding.lineByLine: We read the session cookie; if missing we build a /login URL with a `from` param and redirect. If present, NextResponse.next() lets the request continue and we attach a security header to the response. config.matcher restricts middleware to /dashboard paths so it doesn't run elsewhere.

alternativeApproaches.title: Lightweight JWT verify at the edge
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Verify the token with an edge-compatible library (Web crypto) instead of mere presence, while still doing full checks server-side.
alternativeApproaches.code: import { jwtVerify } from 'jose'; // edge-safe, uses Web crypto

followUps.question: How would you turn this into an A/B test instead of a gate?
followUps.answer: Read/set a bucket cookie and use NextResponse.rewrite(new URL('/variant-b', request.url)) so the URL stays the same.

systemDesign.question: Design edge middleware for a global multi-tenant SaaS that needs auth gating, locale routing, and A/B experiments — all on every request. How do you keep it fast and correct?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Run a single, tightly-scoped middleware at the edge that does only cheap work: read cookies/headers once, do a lightweight (edge-safe) session check, resolve locale, assign/read an A/B bucket cookie, then either redirect (auth) or rewrite (locale + variant) and continue. Scope it with a precise matcher excluding assets/_next, keep the bundle tiny (no Node libs), persist experiment buckets via cookies for stickiness, and push all heavy verification/data work to route handlers/server components. Layer a CDN cache for static/edge responses and ensure rewrites preserve canonical URLs for SEO.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An edge gateway that composes auth, i18n, and experimentation in one pre-render pass.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: These concerns are global and latency-sensitive; doing them at the edge avoids per-page duplication and origin round-trips.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Order matters: (1) matcher filters paths; (2) read inputs (cookies/Accept-Language/geo) once; (3) auth gate -> redirect if needed; (4) locale + bucket -> single rewrite to /{locale}/{variant-or-path}; (5) set sticky cookies + security headers on the response. Everything stays O(1) and edge-safe.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It's a realistic senior design problem: combining cross-cutting concerns at the edge without slowing every request or breaking SEO/statefulness.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A request for /pricing: middleware confirms the session, detects 'fr', reads bucket 'B', and rewrites to /fr/pricing-variant-b while the URL stays /pricing.

nestedTopics.title: Ordering & single rewrite
nestedTopics.explanation: Compute locale and variant first, then perform ONE rewrite to avoid conflicting responses.

nestedTopics.title: Stickiness via cookies
nestedTopics.explanation: Persist the A/B bucket and locale in cookies so users stay consistent across requests.

nestedTopics.title: Edge budget
nestedTopics.explanation: Keep the bundle small and avoid Node APIs/DB calls so middleware adds negligible latency to all traffic.

nestedTopics.title: Caching & SEO
nestedTopics.explanation: Use rewrites (not redirects) for variants to keep canonical URLs, and cache static responses at the CDN.

followUps.question: How do you avoid skewing experiment metrics with bots/crawlers?
followUps.answer: Detect bot user-agents and serve the control variant (or skip bucketing), and don't set experiment cookies for them.

followUps.question: What's the failure mode if middleware throws?
followUps.answer: A thrown error fails the request; design defensively with try/catch and fall back to NextResponse.next() so a non-critical feature can't take down the app.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Treat middleware as a thin edge gateway: one file, precise matcher, ordered logic (auth -> locale -> experiment -> headers), and a single rewrite/redirect decision. Delegate heavy work (DB, full token verification) to route handlers and server components.
productionDeepDive.performance: It runs on the critical path of every matched request, so keep it O(1), bundle-light, and edge-safe. Scope matchers to exclude _next/static, _next/image, and assets so it doesn't run where it isn't needed.
productionDeepDive.security: Use it to enforce auth gates and set security headers/CSP nonces globally, but treat it as defense-in-depth — still authorize data access on the server. Never embed long-lived secrets where they could leak via headers/cookies.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Edge execution scales horizontally close to users with fast cold starts; because it can't hold state, persist experiment/locale decisions in cookies and keep per-request cost minimal so it scales with traffic.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Centralizing cross-cutting concerns in one tested file beats scattering checks across pages; document the matcher and the decision order so reviewers understand why a request is redirected or rewritten.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log/redirect-rewrite decisions and monitor edge latency and error rates (e.g. Vercel edge logs/analytics); watch that middleware time stays low since it taxes every request.

caseStudies.problem: Auth, locale routing, and A/B tests were duplicated per page, adding origin round-trips and inconsistent behavior.
caseStudies.solution: Consolidated into edge middleware doing cheap checks plus a single rewrite/redirect, with sticky cookies and a tight matcher.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Edge constraints (no Node APIs, must stay light) and added per-request logic vs lower latency and centralized correctness.
caseStudies.lessons: Keep middleware minimal and edge-safe; push heavy work to the server and make experiment/locale decisions sticky via cookies.

keyTakeaways: Middleware is a single middleware.ts function that runs on the Edge runtime BEFORE a matched request completes — ahead of rendering and route handlers.
Scope it with config.matcher; by default it runs on every request, so exclude _next and static assets.
Use NextResponse: next() to continue, redirect() to change the browser URL, rewrite() to serve a different path invisibly (A/B, i18n).
The Edge runtime is Web-APIs-only with tight time/size budgets — no Node built-ins; keep checks cheap and push heavy work to the server.
It's ideal for global concerns: auth gating, redirects/rewrites, A/B testing, i18n, and security headers.
